title: Australian Passport Photo Requirements (Size, Rules and Prints)
metaTitle: Australian Passport Photo Requirements: Size, Rules, Prints
metaDescription: Australian passport photo rules: 2 photos, 35-40 x 45-50 mm, head 32-36 mm, under 6 months old, dye-sublimation prints on 200 gsm glossy paper.
excerpt: Every official rule for an Australian passport photo in one place: size, head height, background, pose, glasses, print quality, babies and medical exemptions.
keyTakeaways: Size: 35-40 mm wide x 45-50 mm high, with 32-36 mm from chin to crown.
The photos must be less than 6 months old.
Prints must be dye-sublimation (not inkjet) on glossy paper of at least 200 gsm.
Use a plain white or light grey background, even lighting and a neutral expression.
No glasses unless they cannot be removed for medical reasons.
intro: **Quick answer:** You need 2 colour photos, 35-40 mm wide x 45-50 mm high, with your head measuring 32-36 mm from chin to crown. They must be less than 6 months old, printed by dye sublimation on glossy paper of at least 200 gsm, and taken against a plain white or light grey background.

> **Important:** The Australian Passport Office recommends a professional passport photo provider and does not recommend online photo services or apps. Use our tool to check or prepare a photo, but always confirm it meets the official guidelines before you apply.
**[Check my photo with the Australian passport photo checker →](/australian-passport-photo-checker)**
Below is every rule from the Australian Passport Office photo guidelines, explained in plain English, with links to our detailed guides on size, babies, common mistakes and where to get your photos.

sections.heading: What are the Australian passport photo requirements at a glance?

subsections.heading: Quick specification table
content:
| Requirement | Official rule |
|---|---|
| Number of photos | 2 |
| Photo size | 35-40 mm wide x 45-50 mm high |
| Head size | 32-36 mm from chin to crown |
| Age of photo | Less than 6 months old |
| Print type | Good-quality colour prints made by dye sublimation (not inkjet) |
| Paper | Heavy-weight, glossy, minimum 200 gsm |
| Background | Plain white or light grey, contrasting with your face |
| Lighting | Even, with no shadows or reflections |
| Expression | Neutral, eyes open, facing the camera (over 3 years old) |
| Glasses | Not allowed unless they cannot be removed for medical reasons |
| Retouching | Not allowed |

subsections.heading: How Australia differs from the UK and US
content: Australia allows a size range, not one fixed size. The UK uses a fixed 35 x 45 mm photo with a 29-34 mm head, so a UK photo can have a head that is too small for Australia. The US uses a 2 x 2 inch square, which is the wrong shape.
Australia also needs printed photos made by dye sublimation. You cannot upload a digital photo for a passport.

subsections.heading: What professional prints means
content: The Passport Office asks for good-quality colour prints made by dye sublimation, on heavy glossy paper of at least 200 gsm. Most home printers are inkjet printers, which do not meet this rule.
Post offices, professional photographers, camera stores and some pharmacies and chain stores can make prints like this.

sections.heading: What size must an Australian passport photo be?

subsections.heading: Photo size: 35-40 mm wide x 45-50 mm high
content: The photo must be between 35 and 40 mm wide, and between 45 and 50 mm high. Width comes first.
A 35 x 45 mm photo is inside the range, and it is the size most providers print.

subsections.heading: Head size: 32-36 mm from chin to crown
content: Measure from the bottom of your chin to the top of your head. On the print, this must be 32-36 mm.
If the head is too small, you were too far from the camera or the photo was cropped too loosely. If it is too big, the framing is too tight.

subsections.heading: Which size should you choose?
content: Any size inside the range is allowed. The head height is the part people get wrong, not the outside size.
Our [Australian passport photo size](/guides/australian-passport-photo-size) guide shows the measurements in mm, cm and inches, and compares them with other countries.

sections.heading: What background and lighting do you need?

subsections.heading: Plain white or light grey background
content: Use a plain white or light grey background with no pattern, texture or objects. It must contrast with your face, so the outline of your head is clear.
If you have very light hair or skin, light grey usually gives better contrast than white.

subsections.heading: Even lighting with no shadows or reflections
content: Light must fall evenly across your face. There should be no shadows on your face or on the background, and no reflections on your skin or glasses.
Uneven lighting is one of the problems shown in the official examples of unacceptable photos.

subsections.heading: Why photos with edited backgrounds fail
content: A background that has been edited or replaced is listed as unacceptable. Editing can leave rough edges around hair and change how your head looks.
Take the photo in front of a real plain background instead.

sections.heading: What pose and expression are allowed?

subsections.heading: Straight on, centred, neutral expression
content: Face the camera straight on, with your face centred and your head not tilted up, down or to the side. Look directly at the camera.
If you are over 3 years old, keep a neutral expression. Smiling, and even a subtle expression, are listed as unacceptable.

subsections.heading: Edges of the face visible and hair off the face
content: Both edges of your face must be clearly visible. Your hair must not cover the edges of your face or your eyes.
Tie long hair back or tuck it behind your ears if it falls forward.

subsections.heading: Eyes open and no red eye
content: Keep both eyes open. Red eye is listed as unacceptable, and you must not remove it by editing, because retouching is not allowed either.
If the camera causes red eye, take a new photo with different lighting.

sections.heading: Can you wear glasses, a head covering or jewellery?

subsections.heading: Glasses: only if medically necessary
content: Glasses are not allowed unless you cannot remove them for medical reasons. Needing glasses to see is not, on its own, a reason to wear them in the photo.
If you must wear them, the frames must not cover your eyes and there must be no reflection on the lenses.

subsections.heading: Religious head coverings (plain, no patterns)
content: Religious head coverings are allowed if they are plain, with no patterns. Your whole face must be visible, from chin to forehead, and both edges of your face must show.
Hats and other non-religious headwear are not allowed.

subsections.heading: Jewellery, piercings, hearing aids and earbuds
content: Jewellery and piercings must not cover your face or reflect light.
Hearing aids are allowed for adults, children and babies. AirPods and other wireless earbuds are not hearing aids, so take them out.

sections.heading: What print quality does the Passport Office require?

subsections.heading: Dye-sublimation prints, not inkjet
content: Your photos must be good-quality colour prints made by dye sublimation. This printing method uses heat to transfer colour, which gives smooth, even tones.
Inkjet prints are not accepted. Lines, streaks and ink marks from printing are listed as unacceptable.

subsections.heading: Glossy paper, minimum 200 gsm
content: Print on heavy-weight, glossy paper of at least 200 gsm. Normal office paper is much thinner than this.
Ask your provider to confirm the paper weight if you are not sure.

subsections.heading: Why home printing does not work
content: Most home printers are inkjet printers, and most home photo paper is not made for dye sublimation. That means home prints are very unlikely to meet the rules.
Read [can you take an Australian passport photo online or at home?](/guides/australian-passport-photo-online) for what you can and cannot do yourself.

sections.heading: What about babies, children and medical exemptions?

subsections.heading: Children under 3
content: Children under 3 may have their mouth open. No one else can be visible in the photo, so a parent's hand or a toy in the frame is not acceptable.
The size, background and print rules are the same as for adults. See our [baby passport photo guide](/guides/australian-baby-passport-photo) for tips.

subsections.heading: Medical certificate or B-11 form
content: If a medical condition means you cannot meet a rule, such as removing glasses, you can support this with a medical certificate or a B-11 form.
Read the official guidelines for how to submit it with your application.

subsections.heading: What happens if your photo is not accepted
content: If your photos do not meet the guidelines, you may be asked for new ones. That can slow down your application.
Checking your photos before you apply is the easiest way to avoid this.

sections.heading: Why are Australian passport photos rejected?

subsections.heading: The most common problems
content: The official guidelines show many examples of unacceptable photos. Common ones include:

- smiling or a subtle expression
- glasses on
- shadows or uneven lighting
- head tilted, turned or looking away
- hair covering the eyes
- a background that is not plain, or has been edited
- a toy or a parent's hand in a baby photo
See all of them, with fixes, in our [Australian passport photo mistakes](/guides/australian-passport-photo-mistakes) guide.

subsections.heading: How to check before you apply
content: Use our [Australian passport photo checker](/australian-passport-photo-checker) to test head height, background, lighting and glasses before you pay for prints, or to check the prints you get back.
The checker cannot test print quality or paper, so confirm those with your provider.

faq.question: Can I take my own Australian passport photo?
faq.answer: You can take the photo, but the Passport Office recommends a professional provider and does not recommend online services or apps. Passports also need 2 dye-sublimation prints on glossy paper of at least 200 gsm, which most people cannot make at home. A professional provider is the safer choice.

faq.question: Can I smile in an Australian passport photo?
faq.answer: No. If you are over 3 years old, you need a neutral expression with your mouth closed. Smiling and a subtle expression are both listed as unacceptable. Children under 3 may have their mouth open, but they should still face the camera straight on.

faq.question: How old can my Australian passport photo be?
faq.answer: Your photos must be less than 6 months old when you apply. This applies to adults, children and babies. If you had photos taken for an earlier application, check the date, and get new ones if more than 6 months have passed or your appearance has changed.

faq.question: Can I use a UK or US passport photo?
faq.answer: Not without checking. A UK photo is 35 x 45 mm, but its head size can be smaller than the 32-36 mm Australia needs. A US photo is a 2 x 2 inch square, which is the wrong shape. Australian photos also need dye-sublimation prints on 200 gsm glossy paper.

faq.question: Do I need two photos?
faq.answer: Yes. The Passport Office asks for 2 photos. They should be identical prints from the same photo, made by dye sublimation on heavy glossy paper. Ask your provider for 2 copies, and keep them flat and clean, because ink marks and damage can make a photo unacceptable.

faq.question: Can I wear glasses in my Australian passport photo?
faq.answer: Only if you cannot remove them for medical reasons. Needing glasses to see is not enough on its own. If you must wear them, the frames must not cover your eyes and the lenses must have no reflections. You can support a medical reason with a certificate or a B-11 form.
